quals-berkeley-2023f-a01.title: Three-term recurrence
quals-berkeley-2023f-a01.body:
From $\cos(n+1)x+\cos(n-1)x=2\cos nx\cos x$ we get
$$2\cos(n+1)x=(2\cos x)(2\cos nx)-2\cos(n-1)x\qquad(n\ge1).$$
Define $T_0(z)=2$, $T_1(z)=z$, and $T_{n+1}(z)=zT_n(z)-T_{n-1}(z)$ for $n\ge1$. Each $T_n$ has integer coefficients, by induction. Also $2\cos0x=2=T_0(2\cos x)$ and $2\cos x=T_1(2\cos x)$, and if $2\cos kx=T_k(2\cos x)$ for $k=n-1,n$, then
$$2\cos(n+1)x=(2\cos x)T_n(2\cos x)-T_{n-1}(2\cos x)=T_{n+1}(2\cos x).$$
So the identity holds for all $n\ge0$ by strong induction. (E.g. $T_2=z^2-2$, $T_3=z^3-3z$.) ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-a01.title: Symmetric functions of $t$ and $1/t$
quals-berkeley-2023f-a01.body:
Let $t=e^{ix}$, so $2\cos nx=t^n+t^{-n}$ and $z=2\cos x=t+t^{-1}$. We show by strong induction that $t^n+t^{-n}$ is an integer polynomial in $t+t^{-1}$. For $n=0,1$ this is clear. For $n\ge2$, by the binomial theorem
$$(t+t^{-1})^n=\sum_{j=0}^n\binom nj t^{n-2j}=(t^n+t^{-n})+\sum_{1\le j<n/2}\binom nj\bigl(t^{n-2j}+t^{-(n-2j)}\bigr)+\Bigl[\tbinom{n}{n/2}\text{ if }n\text{ even}\Bigr].$$
Every term on the right except $t^n+t^{-n}$ is an integer combination of $t^m+t^{-m}$ with $m<n$ (and constants), hence an integer polynomial in $z$ by induction. Solving for $t^n+t^{-n}$ shows it is too. ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-a02.title: Local control plus compactness
quals-berkeley-2023f-a02.body:
Let $|f_n|\le K$ for all $n$. For each $x$, $g_n(x)$ is nondecreasing in $n$ and bounded by $K$, so $g_n(x)\uparrow g(x):=\sup_nf_n(x)$.

Let $\epsilon>0$. For each $x\in X$:
- choose $N_x$ with $g(x)-g_{N_x}(x)<\epsilon$;
- by equicontinuity at $x$, choose an open neighbourhood $U_x$ of $x$ with $|f_m(y)-f_m(x)|<\epsilon$ for all $m$ and all $y\in U_x$.

For $y\in U_x$: each $f_m(y)<f_m(x)+\epsilon\le g(x)+\epsilon$, so $g(y)\le g(x)+\epsilon$. And for $n\ge N_x$, $g_n(y)\ge g_{N_x}(y)\ge g_{N_x}(x)-\epsilon>g(x)-2\epsilon$ (as $g_{N_x}$ is a max of finitely many functions each moving by less than $\epsilon$). Hence
$$0\le g(y)-g_n(y)<3\epsilon\qquad(y\in U_x,\ n\ge N_x).$$
By compactness, $X=U_{x_1}\cup\dots\cup U_{x_r}$. With $N=\max_iN_{x_i}$ we get $0\le g-g_n<3\epsilon$ on all of $X$ for $n\ge N$. So $g_n\to g$ uniformly.

**Without equicontinuity.** On $X=[0,1]$ let $f_n(x)=\min(1,nx)$. These are continuous, bounded by $1$, and increasing in $n$, so $g_n=f_n$. Pointwise, $g_n(0)=0$ and $g_n(x)\to1$ for $x>0$. The limit is discontinuous at $0$, while each $g_n$ is continuous, so the convergence is not uniform (a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous). Indeed $g_n(1/(2n))=\tfrac12$, so $\sup|g-g_n|\ge\frac12$. ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-a03.title: A lower bound on $dx/dt$
quals-berkeley-2023f-a03.body:
The right-hand side is smooth, so a unique solution exists on a maximal interval $[0,T^*)$. Whenever $|x(t)|\le1$,
$$x'(t)=1+\tfrac12x^2\sin y\ge1-\tfrac12=\tfrac12 .$$

Let
$$\tau=\sup\{t\in[0,T^*):\ |x(s)|\le1\text{ for all }s\in[0,t]\}>0 .$$
On $[0,\tau)$ we have $x'\ge\frac12$, hence $x(t)\ge\frac t2\ge0$.

*Case $\tau=T^*$.* Then $|x|\le1$ on $[0,T^*)$, so $|y'|=|3-x^2|\le3$ and the solution stays bounded on bounded time intervals; a solution of a smooth autonomous system that stays bounded can be continued, so $T^*=\infty$. But then $x(t)\ge t/2>1$ for $t=3$, contradicting $|x|\le1$. So this case is impossible.

*Case $\tau<T^*$.* By continuity and maximality of $\tau$, $|x(\tau)|=1$, and $x(\tau)\ge\tau/2\ge0$, so $x(\tau)=1$. Since $1=x(\tau)\ge\tau/2$, we get $\tau\le2$.

So $x$ reaches the value $1$ at a time $\tau\le2$, and $x'(\tau)\ge\frac12>0$ there, so the curve genuinely crosses the line $x=1$ (from $x<1$ to $x>1$) by time $t=2$. ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-a04.title: Power series
quals-berkeley-2023f-a04.body:
**Uniqueness.** An entire $f$ equals its Maclaurin series $\sum_{k\ge0}a_kz^k$ on $\mathbb C$, and the series may be differentiated termwise. Then $f''(z)=\sum_{k\ge2}k(k-1)a_kz^{k-2}$ and $zf(z)=\sum_{k\ge3}a_{k-3}z^{k-2}$. Comparing coefficients:
$$a_0=f(0)=1,\quad a_1=f'(0)=1,\quad 2a_2=0,\quad k(k-1)a_k=a_{k-3}\ (k\ge3).$$
These determine every $a_k$, so there is at most one entire solution.

**Existence.** Define $a_k$ by these relations; then $a_{3m+2}=0$ and
$$a_{3m}=\prod_{j=1}^m\frac1{3j(3j-1)},\qquad a_{3m+1}=\prod_{j=1}^m\frac{1}{3j(3j+1)} .$$
By induction $0\le a_k\le1/\lfloor k/3\rfloor!$ (each step multiplies by at most $\frac1{6j^2}\le\frac1j$), so $|a_k|^{1/k}\to0$ and the series $f(z)=\sum a_kz^k$ has infinite radius of convergence. It defines an entire function; termwise differentiation shows $f''=zf$ because the coefficients satisfy the recurrence, and $f(0)=a_0=1$, $f'(0)=a_1=1$. ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-a05.title: Liouville applied to $e^{-f}$
quals-berkeley-2023f-a05.body: Let $g=e^{-f}$, an entire function with $|g(z)|=e^{-\operatorname{Re}f(z)}\le1$. By Liouville's theorem $g$ is constant, so $0=g'=-f'e^{-f}$, and since $e^{-f}$ never vanishes, $f'\equiv0$. Thus $f$ is constant. ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-a05.title: A Möbius transformation
quals-berkeley-2023f-a05.body: The map $\phi(w)=\dfrac{w-1}{w+1}$ sends the closed right half-plane $\operatorname{Re}w\ge0$ into the closed unit disc (since $|w-1|\le|w+1|$ there) and is holomorphic there ($w\neq -1$). Then $\phi\circ f$ is entire and bounded by $1$, so it is constant by Liouville. As $\phi$ is injective, $f$ is constant. ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-a06.title: Divisibility and degree count
quals-berkeley-2023f-a06.body:
Let $D=\det A\in\mathbb R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ and $V=\prod_{i>j}(x_i-x_j)$.

**Divisibility.** Fix $i>j$. View $D$ as a polynomial in $x_i$ over $\mathbb R[x_k:k\neq  i]$. Substituting $x_i=x_j$ makes rows $i$ and $j$ equal, so $D|_{x_i=x_j}=0$; by the factor theorem, $(x_i-x_j)\mid D$. The linear polynomials $x_i-x_j$ ($i>j$) are pairwise non-associate irreducibles in the UFD $\mathbb R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, so their product $V$ divides $D$.

**Degrees.** Each term of the Leibniz expansion of $D$ is $\pm\prod_ix_i^{\sigma(i)-1}$, homogeneous of degree $0+1+\dots+(n-1)=\binom n2$. And $V$ is homogeneous of degree $\binom n2$ too. So $D=cV$ for a constant $c$.

**Constant.** The monomial $x_1^0x_2^1x_3^2\cdots x_n^{n-1}$ occurs in $D$ only from the diagonal (identity permutation), with coefficient $1$. In $V=\prod_{i>j}(x_i-x_j)$, to get exponent $n-1$ on $x_n$ we must pick $x_n$ from all $n-1$ factors $x_n-x_j$; then exponent $n-2$ on $x_{n-1}$ forces picking $x_{n-1}$ from all factors $x_{n-1}-x_j$, $j<n-1$; and so on. So this monomial arises in exactly one way, with coefficient $+1$. Hence $c=1$. ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-a06.title: Row reduction and induction
quals-berkeley-2023f-a06.body:
Induct on $n$ ($n=1$: $\det(1)=1$, empty product). Subtract $x_1$ times column $k$ from column $k+1$, for $k=n-1,n-2,\dots,1$ (in that order). Row $i$ becomes $(1,\ x_i-x_1,\ x_i(x_i-x_1),\dots,x_i^{n-2}(x_i-x_1))$, and row 1 becomes $(1,0,\dots,0)$. Expanding along row 1 and pulling out the factor $x_i-x_1$ from each row $i\ge2$,
$$\det A=\prod_{i\ge2}(x_i-x_1)\cdot\det\bigl(x_i^{k}\bigr)_{2\le i\le n,\ 0\le k\le n-2}=\prod_{i\ge2}(x_i-x_1)\prod_{i>j\ge2}(x_i-x_j)$$
by the induction hypothesis, which is $\prod_{i>j}(x_i-x_j)$. ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-a07.title: Norm estimate
quals-berkeley-2023f-a07.body:
Unitary matrices preserve the Euclidean norm. If $(A+B)v=\lambda v$ with $v\neq 0$, then
$$|\lambda|\,\|v\|=\|(A+B)v\|\le\|Av\|+\|Bv\|=2\|v\|,$$
so $|\lambda|\le2$. ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-a08.title: Combine elements of prime-power order
quals-berkeley-2023f-a08.body:
**Lemma.** If $x,y$ commute and have coprime orders $m,n$, then $xy$ has order $mn$.

*Proof.* $(xy)^{mn}=x^{mn}y^{mn}=1$. If $(xy)^k=1$ then $x^k=y^{-k}\in\langle x\rangle\cap\langle y\rangle$, a subgroup whose order divides $\gcd(m,n)=1$; so $x^k=y^k=1$, hence $m\mid k$ and $n\mid k$, so $mn\mid k$. $\square$

**Abelian case.** Write $e(G)=p_1^{r_1}\cdots p_s^{r_s}$. Since $e(G)$ is the lcm of element orders, for each $i$ some element $g_i$ has order $o_i$ with $p_i^{r_i}\mid o_i$. Then $h_i=g_i^{o_i/p_i^{r_i}}$ has order exactly $p_i^{r_i}$. The $h_i$ commute and have pairwise coprime orders, so by the lemma (and induction) $h=h_1h_2\cdots h_s$ has order $p_1^{r_1}\cdots p_s^{r_s}=e(G)$.

**Non-abelian counterexample.** In $S_3$ the element orders are $1,2,2,2,3,3$, so $e(S_3)=\operatorname{lcm}(1,2,3)=6$, but $S_3$ has no element of order $6$ (it is not cyclic). ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-a09.title: Cyclotomic versus pure radical
quals-berkeley-2023f-a09.body:
Recall that for irreducible $h$, $\mathbb Q[x]/(h)$ is a field isomorphic to $\mathbb Q(\alpha)$ for any root $\alpha$ of $h$ (via $x\mapsto\alpha$).

**(a)** Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x^{101}-1}{x-1}=x^{100}+x^{99}+\dots+1$. It is irreducible because $101$ is prime: $f(x+1)=\dfrac{(x+1)^{101}-1}{x}=\sum_{k=1}^{101}\binom{101}kx^{k-1}$ is Eisenstein at $101$ (all non-leading coefficients $\binom{101}{k}$, $1\le k\le100$, are divisible by $101$, and the constant term $101$ is not divisible by $101^2$). Its roots are $\zeta^k$, $1\le k\le100$, with $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/101}$. Hence $\mathbb Q[x]/(f)\cong\mathbb Q(\zeta)$ contains every root $\zeta^k$, so $f=\prod_{k=1}^{100}(x-\zeta^k)$ splits there.

**(b)** Let $g(x)=x^{100}-2$, irreducible by Eisenstein at $2$. Then $\mathbb Q[x]/(g)\cong\mathbb Q(\alpha)$ with $\alpha=\sqrt[100]2\in\mathbb R$, so this field embeds in $\mathbb R$. If $g$ split into linear factors over it, all roots of $g$ (in $\mathbb C$) would be the images of elements of this field under the embedding, hence real. But $g$ has the non-real root $\alpha e^{2\pi i/100}$. So $g$ does not split over $\mathbb Q[x]/(g)$. (In fact only the roots $\pm\alpha$ lie there.) ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-b01.title: Intermediate value theorem and Rolle
quals-berkeley-2023f-b01.body:
**At least three.** $p(-2)=-32+12+3=-17<0$, $p(0)=3>0$, $p(1)=1-6+3=-2<0$, $p(2)=32-12+3=23>0$. By the intermediate value theorem $p$ has a real root in each of $(-2,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(1,2)$.

**At most three.** $p'(z)=5z^4-6$ has exactly two real roots, $\pm(6/5)^{1/4}$. If $p$ had four (or more) distinct real roots, Rolle's theorem would give three distinct real roots of $p'$ between consecutive ones, a contradiction. A repeated real root $r$ would also be a root of $p'$, so $r^4=6/5$ and $p(r)=r\cdot\frac65-6r+3=3-\frac{24}{5}r$, which vanishes only for $r=\frac58$, but $(5/8)^4\neq \frac65$. So the real roots are simple and there are exactly three. ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-b02.title: Remove the jumps
quals-berkeley-2023f-b02.body:
**The jumps.** A nondecreasing $f$ has one-sided limits $f(x^\pm)$ everywhere (set $f(0^-)=f(0)$, $f(1^+)=f(1)$), with $f(x^-)\le f(x)\le f(x^+)$, and $f$ is discontinuous at $x$ iff the jump $J(x)=f(x^+)-f(x^-)>0$. For distinct points $y_1<\dots<y_m$ the intervals $(f(y_i^-),f(y_i^+))$ are disjoint subintervals of $[f(0),f(1)]$, so $\sum_iJ(y_i)\le f(1)-f(0)$. Hence for each $k$ there are fewer than $k(f(1)-f(0))+1$ points with $J>1/k$, and the set of discontinuities $\{x_n\}$ is finite or countable, with $\sum_nJ(x_n)\le f(1)-f(0)$.

**The functions $h_n$.** With $l_n=f(x_n^-)$, $r_n=f(x_n^+)$, define
$$h_n(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<x_n,\\ f(x_n)-l_n,&x=x_n,\\ r_n-l_n,&x>x_n.\end{cases}$$
Each $h_n$ is zero below $x_n$, constant above it, and discontinuous only at $x_n$ (since $J(x_n)>0$). As $0\le h_n\le J(x_n)$ and $\sum J(x_n)<\infty$, the series $H=\sum h_n$ converges uniformly on $[0,1]$ (Weierstrass M-test). Put $g=f-H$.

**$g$ is continuous.** By uniform convergence, one-sided limits can be taken termwise: for any $x\in[0,1]$,
$$H(x^+)-H(x)=\sum_n\bigl(h_n(x^+)-h_n(x)\bigr),$$
and $h_n(x^+)-h_n(x)=0$ unless $x=x_n$, in which case it equals $r_n-f(x_n)$. So $H(x^+)-H(x)=f(x^+)-f(x)$ (both are $0$ if $x$ is not a discontinuity), i.e. $g(x^+)=g(x)$. Similarly $H(x)-H(x^-)=f(x)-f(x^-)$, so $g(x^-)=g(x)$. Hence $g$ is continuous on $[0,1]$, and $f=g+\sum_nh_n$. (Moreover $g$ is nondecreasing.) ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-b03.title: Integration by parts twice
quals-berkeley-2023f-b03.body:
Since $\frac{d}{dx}\frac{e^{i\lambda x}}{i\lambda}=e^{i\lambda x}$ and $\varphi(1)=\varphi(2)=0$,
$$\int_1^2e^{i\lambda x}\varphi(x)\,dx=\Bigl[\frac{e^{i\lambda x}}{i\lambda}\varphi\Bigr]_1^2-\frac1{i\lambda}\int_1^2e^{i\lambda x}\varphi'(x)\,dx=-\frac1{i\lambda}\int_1^2e^{i\lambda x}\varphi'(x)\,dx .$$
Integrating by parts again, using $\varphi'(1)=\varphi'(2)=0$ and that $\varphi'$ is $C^1$,
$$\int_1^2e^{i\lambda x}\varphi'(x)\,dx=-\frac1{i\lambda}\int_1^2e^{i\lambda x}\varphi''(x)\,dx .$$
Therefore
$$\left|\int_1^2e^{i\lambda x}\varphi(x)\,dx\right|=\frac{1}{\lambda^2}\left|\int_1^2e^{i\lambda x}\varphi''(x)\,dx\right|\le\frac{1}{\lambda^2}\int_1^2|\varphi''(x)|\,dx,$$
so $C=\max\bigl(1,\int_1^2|\varphi''|\bigr)$ works (it is finite because $\varphi''$ is continuous on $[1,2]$). ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-b04.title: Compute the side lengths
quals-berkeley-2023f-b04.body:
Since $|a|=|b|=1$, $|a\pm b|^2=2\pm2\operatorname{Re}(a\bar b)$. From $a+b=-c$ we get $|a+b|^2=1$, so $\operatorname{Re}(a\bar b)=-\frac12$ and
$$|a-b|^2=2+1=3 .$$
The hypotheses are symmetric in $a,b,c$, so likewise $|b-c|=|c-a|=\sqrt3$. In particular the three points are distinct, and the triangle with vertices $a,b,c$ has all sides equal to $\sqrt3$: it is equilateral. ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-b04.title: Rotate so that $a=1$
quals-berkeley-2023f-b04.body: Multiplying by $\bar a$ (a rotation) preserves all hypotheses and the shape of the triangle, so assume $a=1$. Then $b+c=-1$: $\operatorname{Im}b=-\operatorname{Im}c$ and $\operatorname{Re}b+\operatorname{Re}c=-1$. Points on the unit circle with opposite imaginary parts have equal or opposite real parts; opposite real parts would sum to $0\neq -1$, so $\operatorname{Re}b=\operatorname{Re}c=-\frac12$. Hence $\{b,c\}=\{-\frac12\pm\frac{\sqrt3}2i\}=\{e^{\pm2\pi i/3}\}$, and $1,e^{2\pi i/3},e^{-2\pi i/3}$ are the vertices of an equilateral triangle. ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-b05.title: Uniform convergence to $e^{1/z}$
quals-berkeley-2023f-b05.body:
For $|z|\ge\rho$ put $w=1/z$, so $|w|\le1/\rho$ and $f_n(z)=P_n(w)$ with $P_n(w)=\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{w^k}{k!}$, the partial sums of $e^w$. On the compact disc $|w|\le1/\rho$ the partial sums converge uniformly to $e^w$, and
$$|e^w|=e^{\operatorname{Re}w}\ge e^{-1/\rho}=:m>0 .$$
Choose $N$ with $|P_n(w)-e^w|<m$ for all $n\ge N$ and $|w|\le1/\rho$. Then for $n\ge N$ and $|z|\ge\rho$,
$$|f_n(z)|\ge|e^{1/z}|-|f_n(z)-e^{1/z}|>m-m=0 .$$
So for $n\ge N$, every zero of $f_n$ satisfies $|z|<\rho$. ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-b06.title: Explicit eigenvector
quals-berkeley-2023f-b06.body:
The characteristic polynomial is $t^2-(a+d)t+(ad-bc)$, with discriminant $(a+d)^2-4(ad-bc)=(a-d)^2+4bc>0$. So
$$\lambda=\frac{a+d+\sqrt{(a-d)^2+4bc}}{2}$$
is a real eigenvalue, and since $\sqrt{(a-d)^2+4bc}>|a-d|$, we get $\lambda>\frac{a+d+|a-d|}2=\max(a,d)\ge a$.

The vector $v=\begin{pmatrix}b\\\lambda-a\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies the first row of $(A-\lambda I)v=0$: $(a-\lambda)b+b(\lambda-a)=0$. Since $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue, $A-\lambda I$ is singular and nonzero (its off-diagonal entry $b\neq 0$), so its rows are proportional and $v$, which is nonzero, lies in its kernel. Both coordinates $b>0$ and $\lambda-a>0$ are positive. ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-b06.title: Fixed point on the space of directions
quals-berkeley-2023f-b06.body: For $\theta\in[0,\pi/2]$ let $u(\theta)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$. Since all entries of $A$ are positive, $Au(\theta)$ has both coordinates $\ge0$ and is nonzero, so it has a direction $\phi(\theta)\in[0,\pi/2]$, depending continuously on $\theta$. Because $b,c>0$, $Au(0)=(a,c)$ and $Au(\pi/2)=(b,d)$ have both coordinates positive, so $\phi(0)>0$ and $\phi(\pi/2)<\pi/2$. The continuous function $\phi(\theta)-\theta$ is positive at $0$ and negative at $\pi/2$, so it vanishes at some $\theta_0\in(0,\pi/2)$. Then $Au(\theta_0)$ is a positive multiple of $u(\theta_0)$, an eigenvector with both coordinates positive. ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-b07.title: Count ordered bases
quals-berkeley-2023f-b07.body:
**1.** Choosing a basis, $V\cong\mathbb F_q^n$, so $|V|=q^n$.

**2.** An $n\times n$ matrix is nonsingular iff its columns $v_1,\dots,v_n$ are linearly independent. Choose them in order: $v_1$ can be any nonzero vector ($q^n-1$ choices); given independent $v_1,\dots,v_i$, the next column must avoid their span, which has $q^i$ elements, leaving $q^n-q^i$ choices. Hence
$$|GL_n(\mathbb F_q)|=(q^n-1)(q^n-q)(q^n-q^2)\cdots(q^n-q^{n-1}) .$$

**3.** $\det:GL_n(\mathbb F_q)\to\mathbb F_q^\times$ is a homomorphism, surjective since $\operatorname{diag}(t,1,\dots,1)$ has determinant $t$. Its kernel is $SL_n(\mathbb F_q)$, so
$$|SL_n(\mathbb F_q)|=\frac{|GL_n(\mathbb F_q)|}{q-1}=\frac{(q^n-1)(q^n-q)\cdots(q^n-q^{n-1})}{q-1}. $$ ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-b08.title: Action on cosets
quals-berkeley-2023f-b08.body:
**Existence.** $G$ acts by left multiplication on the set $G/H$ of $5$ left cosets, giving a homomorphism $\pi:G\to\operatorname{Sym}(G/H)\cong S_5$. Its kernel $K=\bigcap_{g\in G}gHg^{-1}$ is normal in $G$, and $K\subseteq H$ (an element fixing the coset $H$ lies in $H$). By the first isomorphism theorem $[G:K]=|\pi(G)|\le|S_5|=120$.

**Sharpness.** Let $G=S_5$ and $H=\{\sigma\in S_5:\sigma(5)=5\}\cong S_4$, of index $5$. The normal subgroups of $S_5$ are $1$, $A_5$, $S_5$ (a normal subgroup $N$ meets the simple group $A_5$ in $1$ or $A_5$; if $N\cap A_5=1$ then $|N|\le2$, and a normal subgroup of order $2$ would be central, but $Z(S_5)=1$). Neither $A_5$ (order $60>24$) nor $S_5$ lies in $H$. So the only normal subgroup of $G$ contained in $H$ is $\{1\}$, of index $120$. ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-b09.title: Multiply by the index
quals-berkeley-2023f-b09.body: Let $H\le\mathbb Q$ have finite index $n$. The quotient $\mathbb Q/H$ is a group of order $n$, so by Lagrange's theorem $n(x+H)=H$, i.e. $nx\in H$, for every $x\in\mathbb Q$. Given any $y\in\mathbb Q$, apply this to $x=y/n$: $y=n\cdot\frac yn\in H$. So $H=\mathbb Q$ and the index is $1$. ∎

quals-berkeley-2023f-b09.title: Divisible groups
quals-berkeley-2023f-b09.body: $\mathbb Q$ is divisible: for every $y$ and $m\ge1$ there is $x$ with $mx=y$. Quotients of divisible groups are divisible. A nontrivial finite group $F$ of order $n$ is not divisible: for $y\neq 0$, every $x$ has $nx=0\neq  y$. So every finite quotient $\mathbb Q/H$ is trivial, i.e. $H=\mathbb Q$. ∎
